Name: Dr. Samendra Sherchan
Title: Professor; PI, RCMI Research Project 1
Highlight Text: Recognized for extensive experience working with communities affected by extreme weather events and natural disasters in the US and low-income countries such as Haiti and Nepal.
Bio: Dr. Samendra Sherchan currently serves as the interim director of the Center for Urban and Coastal Climate Research. Dr. Samendra Sherchan is a full professor in the department of Biology at Morgan State University and an adjunct research professor at Tulane University School of Public Health and Tropical Medicine. He also serves as the director of two centers – the Center for Climate Change and Health and the Center of Research Excellence in Wastewater Based Epidemiology. He received his PhD from the University of Arizona. He was a tenured faculty member in the department of Environmental Health Sciences at Tulane University before moving to Morgan State University. In addition, over the past 15 years, he has gained considerable experience working with communities affected by extreme weather events and natural disasters in the US and other low-income countries such as Haiti and Nepal. He was also selected as a NIH Climate and Health Scholar in 2022-2023. He has published over 170 peer-reviewed articles, many in top-tier journals such as ACS EST, Water Research, STOTEN, Lancet etc. He has served as the PI or co-PI for several grants including from NSF, NIH, NOAA, EPA, USGS and private foundations like Gates Foundation. He currently serves as an associate editor for the Journal of Water and Health, AEESP, Medical Microbiology, Total Environmental Microbiology and BMC Infectious Diseases. He is also on the editorial boards of ACS Water, Pathogens, CSCEE and Science of the Total Environment. He is an experienced administrator, scholar, and professor with a proven track record in higher education, skilled in leadership, grant writing, data analysis, mentoring, and community engagement.
Achievements:
Published over 170 peer-reviewed articles, including in ACS ES&T, Water Research, STOTEN, and The Lancet.
Selected as a NIH Climate and Health Scholar (2022–2023).
Served as PI or co-PI on grants from NSF, NIH, NOAA, EPA, USGS, and private foundations including the Gates Foundation.
Google Scholar H-Index of 48 with over 9,000 citations.
Funding Highlights: PI/co-PI on grants from NSF, NIH, NOAA, EPA, USGS, and private foundations including the Gates Foundation.

Name: Dr. Ingrid K. Tulloch
Title: Associate Professor of Psychology and Psychometrics; PI, RCMI Research Project 2
Education 1: B.A. in Psychology and the Interdisciplinary Thomas Hunters Program, Hunter College
Education 2: Ph.D. in Biological Psychology and Behavioral Neuroscience, The City University of New York Graduate School
Education 3: NIDA/NIH Postdoctoral Fellowship (molecular mechanisms of methamphetamine use disorders)
Highlight Heading: Former Psi Chi Eastern Region Vice President
Highlight Text: Also served as President of the Delaware Valley Association of Black Psychologists; leads the Neurobiology of Risky Health Behavior Lab and mentors future biomedical and behavioral scientists.
Bio:
Dr. Ingrid K. Tulloch is an Associate Professor of Psychology and Psychometrics and NIH-supported researcher in the Center for Urban Health Disparities Research and Innovation, and the Center for Brain Health at Morgan State University. Her research uses behavioral and cellular-molecular approaches to investigate biological, psychological, and social factors underlying risky and resilient health behaviors, including substance use and social stress. She earned her B.A. in Psychology and the Interdisciplinary Thomas Hunters Program from Hunter College, and Ph.D. in Biological Psychology and Behavioral Neuroscience from The City University of New York Graduate School, followed by a NIDA/NIH postdoctoral fellowship studying molecular mechanisms of methamphetamine use disorders. A former Psi Chi Eastern Region Vice President and Delaware Valley Association of Black Psychologists President, she leads the Neurobiology of Risky Health Behavior Lab and mentors future biomedical and behavioral scientists.

Research Description: Cross-species research suggests that social threat responses involve underlying neuroimmune components. These biological responses, however, are modulated by demographics, social context, and prior experience. Dr. Tulloch's research encompasses animal models and current translational work in humans to elucidate the dynamic interactions among social experiences, immune activity, and behavior. The goal of this interdisciplinary approach is to understand how experiences contribute to disease risk and resilience.
Achievements:
Former Psi Chi Eastern Region Vice President.
Former President, Delaware Valley Association of Black Psychologists.
Leads the Neurobiology of Risky Health Behavior Lab.

Name: Dr. Timothy Meeker
Title: Assistant Professor; PI, RCMI Research Project 3

Education 3: M.S. in Biological Sciences, University of Cincinnati (2011)

Bio: Dr. Timothy J. Meeker is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Biology at Morgan State University and Principal Investigator of RCMI@Morgan Research Project 3. He earned his Ph.D. in Neural and Pain Sciences from the University of Maryland, Baltimore in 2017, mentored by Dr. Joel Greenspan, and completed a postdoctoral fellowship in the Department of Neurosurgery at Johns Hopkins Hospital in 2022. His research examines the neural mechanisms underlying racial disparities in pain sensitivity, the role of anxiety in pain-related attention, and the analgesic potential of non-invasive brain stimulation. Dr. Meeker is the Principal Investigator of an NIH/NIMHD-funded (U54MD013376) randomized controlled trial evaluating transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) as a treatment for painful chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, and also leads an ASCEND@MSU pilot study on sensory testing in diabetic neuropathy across racial groups. He is a recipient of an NIH/NINDS Loan Repayment Program award (L60NS145314) for work on unbiased diagnostics for neuropathy and neuropathic pain.
Achievements:
Developed a method to make diagnosis of small fiber neuropathy more accessible and less invasive.
Developed lead biomarkers for the efficacy of pain alleviation in patients with neuropathic pain using functional MRI (Ph.D. work).
Demonstrated more detailed evidence for the effect of minoritization on psychological and pain sensory measures.

Spotlight Title: Secondary analysis: heat and self-report pain sensitivity associate with biological sex and racialized sociocultural group but may not be mediated by anxiety or pain catastrophizing
Spotlight Abstract: Previous studies have demonstrated associations between racialized group on pain sensitivity and tolerance. We analyzed the association of sex and racialized group on heat and mechanical pain sensitivity. Using sensory testing for mechanical and heat pain and the pain sensitivity questionnaire (PSQ) we evaluated pain sensitivity in 134 healthy participants self-identifying as white, black or Asian. Racialized minority status was associated with greater heat pain sensitivity (F=7.63; p=0.0007) and PSQ scores (F=15.4; p=9.8×10⁻⁷) but not associated with mechanical pain (F=1.50; p=0.23). Consistent with previous research, sensitivity to painful heat was associated with racialized minority status and female sex. By contrast, there was no significant effect of racialized minority status or female sex on mechanical pain.
